cards.text: This psalm opens on the day Israel departed from Egypt, leaving a people of foreign tongue. Can you imagine finally walking out of a place where nobody speaks your language? Friend, I spent years in a junk drawer next to a pile of takeout menus, and NOT ONE of them spoke cookie.

cards.question: The psalm gives Israel's people another name. It calls them the house of ___.

cards.text: Jacob is the man God renamed Israel (Genesis 35:10). Now his family is out of Egypt, and the psalm says Judah, one of Israel's tribes, became God's sanctuary, and Israel became His dominion.

cards.question: Once Israel is out of Egypt, the psalm says Israel became God's dominion. What does that mean?

cards.text: Then the psalm turns to the sea. The sea takes one look at what's happening and makes a decision REAL quick.

cards.question: When the sea observed what was happening, what did it do?
The sea wasn't the only water on the move. The psalm says the ___ turned back.

cards.text: Next come the mountains and the hills, the world champions of sitting still. They make my years in the junk drawer look like a WORKOUT.

cards.question: What does the psalm say the mountains did?

cards.text: MOUNTAINS. SKIPPING. And the hills right behind them, skipping like lambs, while I hop around on this gold base all day and look about as graceful as a dropped cookie tray.
Then the psalmist does something I do with my oven every morning. He talks straight to them: the sea, the Jordan, the mountains and the hills.

cards.question: The psalmist speaks to the sea, the Jordan, the mountains and the hills. What does he ask them?

cards.text: He doesn't wait around for the sea to answer. He calls out to the whole earth, at the presence of the Lord, the God of Jacob.

cards.question: At the presence of the Lord, the God of Jacob, what does the psalm tell the earth to do?
After asking why the sea fled and the mountains skipped, the psalm points to the presence of the Lord as the answer.

cards.text: The psalm ends with what this God of Jacob did with a rock. A ROCK, friend. Rocks don't do anything. I've shared a drawer with things more lively than a rock.

cards.question: What did the God of Jacob turn the rock into?
The psalm says He also turned the flint into a fountain of water.
The sea flees at His presence, and a rock turns into water. What picture of the God of Jacob does the psalm leave us with?

answers.text: He stays far from His people

findings.problem: The opening card doesn't say who is speaking (the psalmist) or who the psalm is addressed to. It only names the event.

rule.text: The opening card can be up to 3 sentences. It says who is speaking, to whom, and what is going on.

findings.problem: The fill-in-the-blank asks the baker to supply the next word of verse 1 ('house of ___'). No earlier card mentions Jacob, so the baker can only guess. Card 3 explains who Jacob is only after the question, so a new name appears with no introduction.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: The card packs in more than two beats: Jacob renamed Israel, the family out of Egypt, Judah becoming God's sanctuary, and Israel becoming His dominion.

rule.text: Aim for one beat per story card. Two is the most. If a story card has more than two things happening, split it.

findings.problem: The card says Judah is one of Israel's tribes, a Bible fact from outside the passage, but gives no reference for it.

rule.text: Every Bible fact he states carries its reference.

findings.problem: The fill-in-the-blank asks the baker to supply the name in the next line ('the ___ turned back'). Nothing on card 5 or card 6 points to the Jordan, so this is a word guess, not reasoning.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: The card asks the baker to guess the wording of the line ('skipped like rams' vs 'bowed like servants' vs 'melted like wax'). Card 8 only says the mountains usually sit still, which fits all three answers. This is the guessing-a-detail pattern the Psalm 23 example rules out.

rule.text: Ask about the movement and the meaning: what changes, what the picture is, why the speaker says what he says.

findings.problem: The question covers the sea, the Jordan, the mountains and the hills. The right answer, 'Why they fled and skipped', isn't true for the Jordan, which turned back (Psalm 114:5). The right answer also repeats wording from earlier cards while both wrong answers are new, so it stands out.

rule.text: A card about two groups needs an answer true for both. When a question covers more than one group, like the sea creatures and the birds, the right answer must be true for every group in it.

findings.problem: The card says the psalmist calls out to 'the whole earth'. Verse 7 says 'O earth', so 'whole' stretches the text.

rule.text: Don't stretch the text. Exaggerate only in his own jokes.

findings.problem: Card 13 gives nothing that points to 'Tremble' over 'Rejoice'. Mountains and hills skipping like rams and lambs could just as easily suggest joy, so the baker can only guess.

rule.text: Before each choice card, Papa Dorin's story card gives enough context that the baker can reason their way to the answer.

findings.problem: The card asks the baker to guess what the rock became (pool vs tower vs altar). Card 16 gives no hint toward water, so this is a guessed detail, like the oil example in the Psalm 23 table.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: Both wrong answers ('Nature is stronger than Him', 'He stays far from His people') are plainly against the psalm and against God's character, so the right answer stands out and the card is easy without understanding the passage.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: Of the 11 choice cards, about 5 can't be reasoned out (cards 2, 7, 9, 14 and 17). That is far more than a few discovery questions, so they aren't outweighed by informed guesses.

rule.text: A few discovery questions are fine. Some moments can't be reasoned out, like where Jonah's ship is headed. A few of those are okay, as long as most choice cards are informed guesses.

findings.problem: Multiple choice makes up 7 of the 11 choice cards, against 2 fill-in-the-blank and 2 true-or-false, so one type dominates the stop by a wide margin.

rule.text: No stop repeats another stop's pattern, and no type dominates a stop by a wide margin.
